utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, we ended yesterday during the cross-examination of the witness. Would you please resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However, before I do that, I'd like to ask that the witness be given the map that he had yesterday, D77.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, I'd like to ask the Chamber for understanding. It is the Defence's position that at the end of my cross-examination, my colleague will also show the witness two documents which are in English and ask a few questions, because these two documents are in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hamill. Yesterday, your last answer had to do with your possibilities when compiling reports on the basis of information about incidents in the territory controlled by the forces of the BH army and where Papa observation posts were. Can you tell us precisely something about the flow of information, that is, the information that you received from patrolling observers to observation posts and then on. How did it go? You told us that you received this information by radio. The Defence would like to know something about the receipt of written information about incidents happening on the Papa side.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The situation on the Papa side was what you might call a mirror image of what was happening on the Lima side in that they had patrols. They had normally approximately five posts during that period, and they reported similarly instantly by radio when shootreps or increps were required. In other words, if there was an incoming fire into their area or if they saw or heard an outgoing fire from their area. So they would report to the headquarters, and again, as I said, we would hear it on the radio. But we were two separate organisations, the Papa and the Lima, although we were on the same radio net. So they reported through their headquarters. They had a commander on their side called Papa 9er in the same way that there was a commander on the Lima side called Lima 9er, and they reported through him and he commanded them. At that stage, the daily report was made out by him, normally around 16.30 hours, in the same way that we made ours out, and they were forwarded to the headquarters where they were compiled as the UNMO report for sector Sarajevo. But there was absolutely no cross-pollination between the Papa and the Lima sides. We only met each other socially, not professionally. This was in order that the factions could retain confidence in the observers who were working on their side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill. The Defence would like to ask you, after you submit your report, and you told us yesterday that you had only edited it from the point of language, what then happens to that report? Who is it sent to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That report was sent directly to the headquarters of the UNMO organisation in Sarajevo. Now, from there, it went two routes. Firstly, it went to sector Sarajevo where it was used as part of the sector Sarajevo report. Sector Sarajevo comprised a headquarters in the PTT building, a number of battalions. There were three at the time; Egyptian, Ukrainian, and French, and the UNMO organisation. But also, the UNMO report went direct to the headquarters of the UNMO organisation for all of UNPROFOR, which was based in Ilidza barracks in Croatia, in Zagreb in Croatia. So there was a twin track, as it were. Through the sector, and from there, to BH command in Kiseljak and on to UNPROFOR headquarters, but also a short route from the UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo direct to the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb where it formed part of their report -- or extracts from it, rather, formed part of their report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill. Can you tell us, in those cases when you heard protests from the Papa side about the actions of the army of Republika Srpska, would those protests be in writing? And who did you forward them to or hand them over to with regard to the headquarters of the Romanija Corps in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The protests that we would get would not be specifically protests. They would be requests. We got requests from the Papa side to use our good offices with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to cause the shelling or sniping to cease. So we would go directly across the hall, five metres, and meet one of the liaison team, whoever was on duty, and request them to get on to the brigade in question to stop the shelling. And this often happened, but not, as I said yesterday, not invariably. Sometimes it was explained to us that the shelling or shooting was in response to an attack on Vojska Republika Srpska positions. And in that case, obviously they were not going to stop until the Papa side had stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have just mentioned the sniping activities, the Defence would like to know if, as an experienced military expert, you can accept that the sniping activity is also the fire opened from other infantry weapons, not only from a rifle with optical sights. I'm basing this question on the fact that you know what a sniper is. Or perhaps would you tell us, what is a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: A sniper, in normal military parlance, is somebody who will target specific individuals at long range and kill them, generally using a rifle with a telescopic sight. Generally, a sniper operates alone from concealment and functions to a certain extent outside a normal military environment in that he doesn't operate as part of a unit. Normally, he's there as an individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, when you say "sniping activities," or "opening fire from infantry weapons," would you call that sniping activity too? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sniping activity is an attempt to kill a specific individual that you see as opposed to more general use of small-arms fire in an attack. It is targeted, it is specific, and it uses the minimum rounds possible to achieve its task, which is to kill a specific individual who has been spotted by the sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So fire from infantry weapons, from small arms, and fire from infantry weapons, you would not call it as sniping activity or the opening of sniping fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not normally, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Lukavica, how did you and did you investigate any sniping activities? Specifically, can you explain to us what would you do after receiving the information that somebody had been hit by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was not possible to do anything for the individual in question, obviously, but what we did is we went into Grbavica and drove up and down in the streets of Grbavica, listening for snipers so that we could report to our comrades on the Papa side through the headquarters that there was sniping going on and that we would request them to intervene with the government forces and cause the sniping to be stopped. So it was a case of not helping the individual who had been shot because it was too late for them, but it was an attempt to prevent any other individuals from being killed. Patrolling up and down the streets, listening, reporting when we heard a sniper shot. Because again, you must remember, as I just mentioned, a sniper fires the minimum possible number of shots for a number of reasons. He wants a first-round kill, because any more than one round involves a danger of giving away his position, and the essence of sniping is shooting from a concealed position where he will not be seen and where he will be able to continue his deadly work. Sniping is intermittent. It doesn't happen bang, bang, bang.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during that period of time when you were there, how many protests did you forward on through liaison officers and which incidents did it concern, specifically protests that you received from the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I cannot be specific. Whenever we got a report in from the Papa side, which happened regularly, that there was a shelling or a shooting incident in a particular area, one of us would go in, sometimes me, sometimes one of my colleagues, to discuss the issue with the liaison officers present and to bring about a ceasefire. Now, I -- at this stage, I cannot say specific incidents, specific dates, but regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Those protests, would they be referring to a specific incident at a specific place or would they be general?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not general, specific. We would be told, "There is shelling going on in a particular area. Please have it stopped." Or, "There is sniping going on in a particular area into a particular area, please have it stopped." Generally, it referred to shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during that period of time, were there any incidents or did you receive any protests related to incidents requiring a particular investigation? If you are telling us that you cannot list those incidents, were there, during this May, June, or July, any incidents that required your particular investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not investigation per se. What we're talking about here is attacks going on in an area which was not monitored by us, which was monitored by observers from the Papa side and which they then reported to us as being incoming fire from our side and requesting us to have the activity stopped. In other words, we didn't investigate what happened on the other side of the line. I didn't cross the line normally except to go into the headquarters. I stayed, as my colleagues on the Lima side did, on the Lima side. It was only when we were reporting into the headquarters in the PTT building that -- in Novi Grad or Novo Sarajevo that we would cross the line normally. There were -- there were exceptions, obviously, but very, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us if, in the area of Dobrinja and Alipasino Polje, there was a Papa observation point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There was a Papa post on a hill overlooking the area, Papa 2 or 5, I cannot remember which. Because again, by convention and by policy, we didn't go to the Papa posts. It was felt better from the point of view of the two parties to the conflict that they would have more confidence in us if we were not mixing with observers who were working on the other side, as it were, and that we required confidence to do our job. So I wasn't specifically aware of the house, for example, that a Papa post would be in. But afterwards, when I was posted in Zagreb as deputy chief operations officer and returned to Sarajevo, I did visit Papa posts, and I noticed one in particular was looking down on the area of Alipasino Polje. Dobrinja would be much further on. There was none specifically in the area of Dobrinja, but patrolling was carried out in the area of Dobrinja. Now, patrolling was also carried out on the Serb side of Dobrinja by our people, and they controlled, for example, in Nedzarici, and also in Aerodromsko Naselje, the airport settlement, because they were areas controlled by Vojska Republika Srpska. So it was a case of operating from a fixed base, but that wasn't the actual observation post. The observation post comprised, in effect, the entire city of Sarajevo and its surroundings, surroundings for us, and the city for the Papa teams. They could be anywhere in that area, and they were required to be generally through the area --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill. In May, June, July, you were in Lukavica. Yesterday, you spoke about an incident which happened in Dobrinja, and you said that in September 2001, you visited that part of Dobrinja. Can you tell us, since during the relevant period of time when that happened, that was the 1st of June, 1993, when did you receive information, when did you learn of that incident of the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I learned it generally at that time in that we were aware of major incidents which occurred in the city and in the surrounding areas because they would have been reported on the press, if nowhere else. CNN gave us a lot of information. But in this particular case on that day, I spent the morning in the headquarters and the afternoon out on one of our posts in the east of the city, Lima 7, which was somewhere in the area of Sombolovac. So I wasn't aware specifically of that incident at that time when it happened, but I gained my information shortly afterwards but gave it no great heed, as you might say, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was it that informed you about that incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I can't. It was one of those items which is mentioned on a daily basis. You will remember that I explained that we were actively working from 7.00 in the morning until 11.00 at night, exchanging information with other people, with the headquarters. It was very likely somebody from our own headquarters who told me about the incident, but I couldn't be specific. And again, possibly I heard it on the BBC World service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your post at the time, did you draw up a report on that incident because you were informed about it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And were you shown a report relative to that incident on the 1st of June, just to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Again, as I explained, it was on the Papa side. It was not on the Lima side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But can you then explain -- in relation to that incident which happened in the proximity of your observation posts, can you then explain it to us how is it possible that you received absolutely no report in relation to that incident or protest?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The incident occurred on the Papa side and was reported on by the personnel on that side. It did not happen on my side of the line, therefore, I had no responsibility for reporting on it. The two sides were kept quite separate in regards to the reporting responsibilities. That which happened on the Presidency side was reported on by the teams there. That which happened on the Serb-controlled side was reported on by one of the Lima teams which had responsibility for that area. In the case of the Dobrinja shelling where the football match was shelled, I was, as I said, in the morning in the headquarters on business and in the afternoon, again, on business in the Lima 7 area which was approximately 15 kilometres, I would say, to the east of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Hamill, you are confirming to us that in relation to the incident which happened on the 1st of June, 1993, you, as the head of the team in Lukavica, did not receive any protest related to that incident, nor did you personally submit a written protest in relation to that incident, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: At that time, I was not head of the team. I was the liaison officer. The head of the team was a Norwegian captain who remained there for some time afterwards. I went in as a liaison officer into the headquarters on the UNMOs on the Lukavica side to assist him in his work, being prepared to take over the job from him when the time came. But there was another officer who was the commander of the UNMOs there at that time, not me. I was liaison.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So as the liaison officer, your associates never gave you a written protest in relation to that incident, nor did you forward any such protest to anyone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of my memory, no. But memory -- I simply cannot say that it happened or that it didn't happen. I have no memory of it happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, throughout the month of June specifically, did you have occasion, as the liaison officer, to receive any report whatsoever from monitors about that incident, or perhaps your colleague? You told us he was a Norwegian. Could you tell us his name, please. Did either of you receive any kind of report relating to that incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hamill, while you held that position - I won't repeat it - did you ever receive any information and do you know that in Dobrinja in July, there was an incident when a water line was shelled? Did you receive any report about that while you were the liaison officer in the area under the control of the army of Republika Srpska? Have you heard about that incident at all? Did you, at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: At this stage, I cannot say whether I heard about it at the time or not. I imagine I would have heard when it happened, but that it was just one in a long, long list of incidents. We had major incidents occurring throughout the entire period. We had anything from one thousand to three and a half thousand shells being fired, for example, in a 12-hour period. This would be something which would be of interest and which would stick in your mind. But one shelling, one small shelling, wouldn't stand out after all this time. But I certainly specifically remember times when 3.600 rounds were fired into the city from the north over a 12-hour period. I mean, what you are asking me about is one in a whole litany of shellings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, I'm asking you about these two incidents, the one of the 1st of June and the 12th of July, as we have reports disclosed to us by my learned friends from the Prosecution that on that day, both on the 1st of June and the 12th of July, there were civilian casualties. So I'm asking you when such incidents occurred, such as this shelling of the water line, was it necessary to set up a mixed commission in accordance with international law which should have gone to the spot and established what actually happened in Dobrinja when, according to the report, there were civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no mixed commission was set up at that time for either of those incidents. The first such commission that I remember specifically was that which occurred after the Markale shelling of the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are confirming that you yourself have no knowledge that regarding the incidents of the 1st of June and the 12th of July, which is within your tour of duty, that you personally at any time received a protest regarding those incidents, nor did you forward any such protests --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- to responsible authorities, nor are you aware that any mixed commissions were formed in relation to those incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I neither confirm nor deny that I received or forwarded a protest. I am saying that I do not remember if such a protest was forwarded about those specific incidents at that specific time. We had numerous protests that we forwarded, but they may or may not have been part of those. We were operating, as you will appreciate, on a minute-to-minute basis, and when an incident was reported to us that a particular set of activities was happening in a particular place. We immediately went in across to the liaison office. It was part of daily work. We just went in, informed them, requested them to cause the shelling to be stopped, and either they did or they didn't, and then we went on to the next incident. Very, very few incidents actually stand out. Markale is obviously one because of the scale of it. An incident or an activity where three and a half thousand rounds is fired from 4.00 in the morning until 4.00 in the afternoon obviously stands out. An incident where Lukavica barracks was shelled and you're on the receiving end of it obviously stands out, but this was just one in a whole litany, a whole series of attacks that went on killing civilians in the city of Sarajevo -- or these two, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that you were present when the Lukavica barracks was shelled. Could you tell us when that was and from which positions of the BH army was Lukavica shelled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I cannot say from which position it was shelled, as I didn't see the firing. I just know that it was shelled around the middle of July. I think perhaps -- I think it was actually -- no. It was actually the 4th of July, if I remember right, we were shelled by mortars. Several rounds came in over a period of a number of hours. That was one, one occasion. There was -- there were a few occasion like that. I mean, it happened on an irregular basis. About every couple of weeks, a few shells would fall onto the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about the Lukavica barracks, yesterday you explained where you yourself, as the observers, were stationed, what part of the building you occupied. You said that on the floor above you, General Galic was stationed. Could you tell us, regardless of the fact that you told us that you never went to his premises, could you tell us, in view of the position of the Lukavica barracks, what kind of view does it have of Dobrinja, that is, from the premises where General Galic was, that were used by General Galic? Could you confirm that his offices faced in an opposite direction in relation to Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I can't. What I can say is that the area is very, very flat from Lukavica barracks through Dobrinja, the airport. That's why the airport was built there. But Dobrinja itself comprises buildings which are several storeys high, blocks of flats, and from the second storey of that building, if one were on the south side of it, one could see the area of Dobrinja which was still controlled by Serbs. I would say that it was not possible to see deep into Dobrinja because of the fact that you had high buildings. So all that you could see from there would be the first line of buildings in the distance, maybe a kilometre and a half, two kilometres distant. But you couldn't see through Dobrinja for that reason. Similarly, there was a hill on the right-hand side as one -- as one was facing Dobrinja, facing Lukavica, which ended up at Mojmilo. And this hill provided cover from view for the bulk of area beyond the Serb-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, yesterday you told us about the kind of weapons that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the BH army had in view of your area of responsibility. Did you have any information about the deployment of mortars and guns of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The information that we had was that the mortars were used in a classic pattern, that is, that they were brought to a location, they fired a number of rounds, and then they went away somewhere else so that they remained hidden from view, and they were used with great flexibility. So they didn't actually, as far as I know, leave mortars sited any specific location. They had very, very few resources as far as firepower was concerned. They relied on infantry troops, the reverse of the VRS. So they had to husband their resources carefully and not leave them in a position where they could be hit by counter-battery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, with regard to your area of responsibility, what kind of weapons the BH army had on Mount Igman, and are you aware that there was an observation post at Igman as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Whose observation post?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: A Papa observation post.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not until after Igman had been captured. As far as I know, there were no -- the team was set up sometime, I think, in the end of July. It wasn't there through May and June. I didn't visit them until December. The weapons that the Armija BH had, they certainly included mortars because they would use those to shell Vojkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, since you have now explained how the BH army used those mortars, do you know from which positions the BH army used mortars most frequently?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is my understanding that they used them from numerous positions, including directly outside the UN headquarters in Sarajevo and the grounds of Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you counted the number of shells fell on a particular part of the city and from which positions within a certain period of time. Could you tell us whether you used radars as a means of determining the route of projectiles and the exact spot from which those projectiles were fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, we didn't because we weren't in possession of radars. Radars are useful for slow-flying projectiles such as mortar bombs. They are not useful, in general, for artillery weapons. What we used were our ears. We heard the rounds being fired on the left. We heard them being -- exploding on the right. Therefore, they came from the left and they went to the right. Left was the area of the Kosevo and Vogosca Brigades; right was the area of the city. And similarly, at the same time, the UNMOs in the city were reporting shelling incoming into the city. So it was quite clear; there was no requirement to use radar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in connection with what you told us yesterday about the sound of a mine as it explodes, at what distance, specifically is it one or two kilometres, you can hear the sound of a mortar shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It can be heard [Realtime transcript read in error "fired"] from a very considerable distance. Depending on conditions, depending on the size of the weapon, depending on the type of terrain, it can be heard across a very, very large distance. We're talking about several kilometres. Certainly five, in ideal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether that is a sound that an ordinary man can recognise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a correction perhaps in respect to the last answer. I think I heard the witness say, "It can be heard from a very considerable distance." That was how he started his answer. What I have here is, "It can be fired from a very considerable distance," which I don't think would be his answer, having regard to the context in which -- or having regard to the question that was asked. The question was, "You can hear the sound of a mortar shell being fired at what distance?" So I imagine the answer would be as I heard it: "It can be heard from a very considerable distance." And perhaps that part of the transcript could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we should first clarify. The question was, Mr. Hamill, from what distance you could hear the sound of a mortar shell being fired? And then the answer in the transcript says that it can be fired from a very considerable distance. And it is Mr. Stamp's recollection that you said it can be heard from a very considerable distance. Could you -- my recollection is not -- could you please confirm what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my belief, Mr. President, that I said it can be heard from a very considerable distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is logical if you read the rest of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this will be corrected as far as the transcript is concerned. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, could you tell us, please, whether the sound of a shell being fired can be recognised by an ordinary man?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is an ordinary man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the question is that someone who is not militarily trained, whether they could -- is that what you intended to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: A man who is not a professional and who has no knowledge of military equipment, can he distinguish and recognise the sound of a mortar shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I would say there is absolutely no difference to the untrained ear between any type of explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were telling us about the incident at Dobrinja which you visited, and you said that Mr. Ismet Fazlic identified two craters for you, could you tell us what your conclusions were after examining those craters? You said that there were traces of the wings which are characteristic of craters formed by a gun or a Howitzer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know and were you informed by anyone as to who carried out the on-site identification of those projectiles and whether, when this incident occurred, any remnants of the projectile were found? Were you informed about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was not so informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that your conclusion was that this was a 120-millimetre projectile. Can you tell us on the basis of what did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I said it was most likely a 122-millimetre Howitzer projectile, and I based that on the size of the crater. It was actually quite small, quite shallow. Therefore, it wasn't a powerful explosion. A 120 mortar bomb, for example, would have made a larger mark because it contains more explosive. So it looked to me as a relatively light weapon but still an explosive one. And judging by the wings, it looked to me to be a gun. And when I looked at the area it came from and examined it on the map, I found a location where I knew on that day there were a battery of 122-millimetre guns in situ. And my assumption was that they were the guns that fired those rounds. The marks were consistent with having been made by a gun of that calibre, so it was logical to assume that they were the guns which fired it and that no other gun had come into the same area and had fired at that target at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you used to come to the conclusion that those projectiles were fired from the positions of Lima 5?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The fact that the rounds had come from that direction. I worked out the bearing that they had come in on, and it pointed down to the area of Toplik, plus or minus 5 degrees. On that basis, and on the basis of my knowledge of the area at the time and the weapons that were in it, I formed a conclusion that it was one or more of that battery which had fired those rounds. The rounds certainly came from that direction. And the only guns that were in that area belonged to the VRS, and the only ones that I knew personally of which fit that description were in the area of -- that I outlined yesterday, of Toplik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As you are telling us that it was the area of Toplik, an area where you had your monitors, did they inform you that in June, specifically on the 1st of June, that a gun or Howitzer or mortar had been fired from Lima 5? Do you have in your archives any documents where your associates are informing you that there was firing with guns from that area on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In my own personal archives, I do not. However, if guns were fired on that day from that position, there would be a record in the official UNPROFOR documentation which I'm sure the Court can gain access to. Because it would have been reported as a shootrep by Lima 5, the team in Lima 5 who were in situ on the day, as to the time the firing occurred, how many rounds were fired and in what general direction. So while I do not have access to those records, I'm quite sure that somebody does and can produce them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In September, were you informed that the competent Bosnian authority service had carried out any investigation regarding that incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, I was doing an investigation independently of any other investigation, and I wasn't interested in what other authorities had done. I was purely carrying out a technical analysis, myself, without reference to other persons' information, whether accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, during that period of time when you had an observer post in Toplik, with regard to the location of the incident, could you tell us where the confrontation line was, or the front line between the two warring factions in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The front line in that area generally ran at the base of the hill of Mojmilo down across the front of Lukavica to Dobrinja where the easternmost blocks of flats were on one side of the confrontation and the remainder of the suburb was on the other side of the confrontation line. It ran from there down along the edge of the airport, which was controlled by a French battalion at that stage, but at one end you had -- at the east end you had a VRS tank position down at Kula restaurant, and from there then it kind of wandered off by Butmir and on to Hrasnica. In a northerly direction, the front line went across Mojmilo, down into Hrasno to the stadium, down to the River Miljacka, along the river quite a distance, and then climbed back up so that generally the suburb of Grbavica was in VRS -- under VRS control, and the remainder was not. It went up by the Jewish cemetery and along the base of the hill of Zlatiste and then curved around. On the northern side, it was very, very indeterminate. It was my opinion that there was no front line per se between the eastern part of the city and the VRS-controlled area in Sombolovac. It was generally a no-man's land but difficult terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we are now talking about Dobrinja, and that you have already told us that there was action, firing, from Toplik in the direction of Dobrinja from guns and Howitzers, you told us yesterday that your experience with regard to the Serb shelling was such that always before shells were fired from artillery weapons, members of the observer mission were called. How do you explain that guns and Howitzers were fired in an area where your observation post was situated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I am not saying that the firing was not observed by military observers. If they fired from that position on that day, and if there were UNMOs in situ, they would certainly be aware of it because the guns were very close to the UNMO accommodation. Similarly, as I said yesterday, the battery commander would normally come to the door and say, "We're about to fire. Target is such and such. Would you like to come and have a look?" And the observers who were based in Lima 5 would go and they would examine. They would sight along the barrels. They would check the various instruments on the gun and see which way they were firing. I'm not saying that that did not happen on that day. It may very well have done. I'm not aware that it did; I'm not aware that it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hamill, before you took up your duties in Lukavica, was someone else from the UN there who performed the duties that you took over? And if so, could you tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, there were a team in situ comprising a Norwegian captain and a Russian major, and I joined them as an additional member of the staff preparatory to taking on the role of deputy and then being trained as the commander of the area. However, the UNPROFOR authorities recognised my competence and transferred me elsewhere to a more responsible position. But there would have been no one in the job of liaison officer, but there were two officers living in the same accommodation, working in the same office for a considerable period of time. It is my belief, although I'm not sure, that there was constantly somebody based in the headquarters of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps from its inception, perhaps. Certainly for a considerable period before I came.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So when you all worked together, did you receive information from them that during that time prior to your arrival, prior to your arrival there, there was an attack of the humanitarian aid convoy in Hrasnica and Dobrinja and that, in that column, civilians had been wounded and that that fire had been opened from the direction of Vogosca and Hrasnica? Do you have any knowledge that before you arrived there, there was an action launched from that area against a convoy of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry. You mentioned two areas here, Vogosca and Hrasnica. At that time, Vogosca was under the control of the VRS and Hrasnica was under the control of the armija. Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Hrasnica and Igman. Hrasnica and Igman.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I heard of an incident, but again I have no personal knowledge of it. But it was mentioned to me as part of my initial briefing that such incidents occurred, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information that from the part of the neighbourhood that what -- near the airport controlled by the BH army, that, is the entrance into that tunnel, that there were civilian casualties in that area hit as they were crossing the airport?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: My understanding is that there were civilian casualties. Now, I'm also aware from my own observation that civilians crossed the runway of the airport not just by the tunnel but above ground also. At night. Not by day, at night. And they were shot at. I cannot say, because it was a considerable distance from my room, whether people were hit or not, but we could see figures crossing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, to finish up with the map, could you take the map and mark where was your observation post in relation to Vogosca so that we can round off the area covered by Lima.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Right. Now, there were a number of locations used by the UNMOs during this period. The one that I moved to in early July was in Blazuj, which is off this map. It's on the road -- it's where the road from Kiseljak and the road to Mostar diverge. So I will mark the approximate area. That was the area known to us as Lima 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, just a moment. We need to specify for the record that "L2" -- I can't see what letter is that. So can we say for the record what is the Blazuj area? Could you please put letter "B" next to "Lima 2" --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- so that we can know it is Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Mr. Hamill has written Blazuj beneath "Lima 2," which was the area where the Lima 2 observation team was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, can you tell us, where were the front lines between the two warring sides in that area in relation to Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In relation to Blazuj, it was between two confrontation lines. The Igman and Ilidza Brigades were the two brigades which were monitored by Lima 2, and effectively they operated up to the base of Mount Igman. Ilidza to the east and the Igman Brigade to the west. The Igman Brigade operated out of a location in the village Blazuj itself, and the Ilidza Brigade operated out of a hotel complex not far from Vrelo Bosne. So they were two brigades in that area. Now, to its east also we had another observation post near Rajlovac, and that was Lima 3. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. Later on I will ask you also to indicate where Lima 3 in Rajlovac is, because before that, can you tell us during your tour of duty, do you know if there was any shelling in the areas of Ilidza and Blazuj of that part of the city of Sarajevo from the positions the BH army? And I mean its positions on Igman.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There were shellings in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were -- was there -- were there any attacks from BH positions in relation to this area controlled by the army of Republika Srpska, and was small-arms fire and sniper fire opened against these areas? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: What happened in that area during my period there was a major attack which seemed to us, and again I must emphasise it seemed to us, to be initiated by the armija on Igman. And it was responded to in the main by the two brigades that I have -- I've mentioned, the Ilidza Brigade and the Igman Brigade. And Colonel Cojic, the Commander of the Igman Brigade, brought his men successfully to the top of Igman and effectively captured Igman from the armija. But as I say, it seemed to us at the time that the activity had been initiated by the army of BH rather than by the VRS. The VRS then took advantage of the situation to continue onwards and capture Igman. That would have been mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill. Can you mark on the map the area that you said was covered by Lima 3 and that it was the area of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Now, I cannot be specific on this, but this is the Rajlovac area, and the team was on a hill overlooking it somewhere around there. Again, I cannot be specific on this particular occasion. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, for the record, I will say that under Lima 3 -- you indicated Lima 3 observation post, and under it you've placed the letter "R" to indicate that it was the area of Rajlovac. During your tour of duty there, can you tell us if, from the positions of the BH army, there was any fire opened against Rajlovac, and can you tell us which are the positions which the BH army held in relation to Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In relation to Rajlovac, the BH army was on this hill feature looking down onto Rajlovac. Now, the front line would have been somewhere in that area, but that's only very, very roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if during that period of time when you were there, did you have any knowledge of any fighting during that time and whether there were any combat operations between the two armies and how often did that happen? Did you receive any reports to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. This was a very, very active area. There was -- there were constantly warring activities going on in the area, infantry attacks by the armija against the RS positions in an attempt to break through and break the hold that the VRS had on Sarajevo. It was very, very active.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in this area which you have marked as a hill and a square saying "BH," whether this is the area of Brijesce Brdo and Sokolje Brdo area, and do you know which BH army's formation held that part of the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is Brijesce Brdo, but I don't know who specifically held it on the armija side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, have you just marked on this map all of the Lima posts in the part of the city controlled by the troops, by the forces of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I have not. There are more. Lima 11, Lima 1-1, was in constant contact with the Vogosca Brigade and was based in a house overlooking the Vogosca area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Mr. Hamill has, under Lima number 11, marked the observation post and the area of Vogosca where this observation post was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, can you tell us concerning the neighbourhood of Vogosca, was that part of the city of Sarajevo exposed to the attacks of the BH army from Hotonj, Zuca and Vulic [phoen], and were those lines where there were frequent conflicts and exchanges of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. There were very, very frequent conflicts and exchanges of fire in that area as the armija had position which overlooked Vogosca and indeed which could be seen clearly from the position Lima 1-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, can you confirm for us whether during your stay in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sarajevo and during your tour of duty there, and after we've identified the positions of your observation posts, can you confirm for us that the hills and elevations such as the hill of Mojmilo, Mount Igman, Brijesce Hill, then hills of Zuc, Osnicina [phoen], Hotonj, and Orlic, that throughout the conflict, they were under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the location of Orlic, but the remainder were certainly throughout the entire period under the control of Armija BH. Perhaps if you tell me where Orlic is, I can confirm that, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is near the hill, Zuc hill.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, we're not finished. There was another team to the east of Lima 1-1 in the area of Radava who had liaison with the Kosevo Brigade. I don't believe that it's on this map, but I will indicate generally where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Hamill has put "L-12" to indicate the observation post Lima 12 which was in the area of Radava. In relation to the Radava area, Mr. Hamill, can you tell us something concerning the front line. You tell us that this area was controlled by the Kosevo Brigade. In relation to which part of this area, how far were the positions of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The BH army was much further down in this area. Now, we did not have good access to this area. It was difficult to get teams in and out. There was a lot of suspicion of our team by the leadership of the brigade, and we did not have good cooperation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the positions of the BH army in relation to your observation post at Radava, when you say that they were at the foot, does it mean that they were in the area of Sedam Suma, Grdonj, and the hill of Hum?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the front line would have been somewhere in the area of Sedam Suma.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And is it where the Grdonj -- where that hill is also located next to Sedam Suma?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill. Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Could I say, I was in that area only once, so my knowledge of what went on that area would be very, very limited. We had severe problems in that area, as I said, with establishing relationships, and we were chased out of it on more than one occasion. We had severe restrictions of movement imposed on us by both the VRS and their irregular allies, the so-called Chetniks. So it was difficult to find out exactly what was happening in that area. There was one other team farther to the east in the area of Sombolovac, as I mentioned. That was team Lima 7, much further to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And you can't mark it on this map here, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. Also during my period, we established a team in Grbavica. If you wish, I can mark that also.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hamill. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The team was accommodated in the position shown on the map, shown as Lima 6 Grbavica, but they operated exclusively within the Grbavica area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill. Mr. Hamill, on the 5th of December, 1993, you were on Mr. McEvoy's [Realtime transcript read in error "McEnvoy"] team, doing a round of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: On that day, I was down for a conference in Kiseljak, and I took the opportunity to have a look at the Papa side of the city and was brought around by a John McEvoy, not McEnvoy. There is a misprint. So McEvoy. He brought me around the various parts of the Papa area which, of course, was very interesting for me as it was almost new territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you visited the Kosevo Hospital on that occasion and how Mr. McEvoy explained to you on that occasion and showed to you the part of the hospital when two nurses and a doctor were killed by a shell? Did you have an opportunity to see the damage done then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during the examination of the damage done on that occasion, could one see the craters caused by the projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: There was one hole in the wall. It was a circular hole, quite large. I think at this distance I would say probably a metre across, and it was almost perfectly circular.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, with regard to the examination of that part of the building which was damaged and the damage was caused by a shell, what were the conclusions that you arrived at? Could you establish precisely from which positions could have been fired the projectile which damaged that part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The damage was pointed out to me as having been caused by a mortar bomb. However, when I examined it, I didn't do it closely, but it seemed very clear to me that it had been caused by a flat trajectory shell; that is, one which came in almost horizontal to the ground and caused a circular explosion rather than a shaped hole that one might have expected if the round had come in downwards. So it seemed to me to be a high-velocity, direct-fire weapon such as would be used on a tank. I felt it was almost certainly a tank round. And there was -- from that point of view, I looked around, and I could see no positions occupied by the VRS that could have fired a tank round at that building at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that with regards to the examination of the crater caused by the shell in the hospital, that on the basis of that examination, one cannot confirm that it was fired from the area under the control of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was my opinion that it was not fired from the area under the control of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but rather fired from within the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say from the positions within the city, do you mean by that - can you confirm for us - that it could have been also done from mobile mortars used by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, not mortars. Tank. Not a mortar. It was not a mortar round, in my view. It didn't appear to have the characteristics that one would expect even from an explosion on a wall from a mortar round. It appeared to be, to me, to be a direct-fire, flat-trajectory weapon, such as a field gun or, more likely, a tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, do you have any knowledge whether in the vicinity of the Kosevo Hospital, the BH army in the area of the tunnel which is near the hospital, that it had a tank there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge with regards to the Kosevo Hospital where were the positions of the BH army which had a tank? Do you know which --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and by their nature, they move on a regular basis. And as I mentioned earlier on, it would not have been the policy of an organisation with scarce resources to squander those by leaving them exposed to counter-battery fire or to leave them in positions which would make them open to attack. So really the question is not relevant. A tank, of its nature, moves.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see it is time for a break. I will have a few more questions to ask in relation to the incident which Mr. Hamill investigated at Markale, but I believe this would be a convenient time for break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I just ask you, as you might have noticed, I did not interrupt you in order to indicate to you that the cross-examination took already more time than the examination-in-chief. I did not want to interrupt you at that very moment. How much time would you still need, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 10 minutes, say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how much time would Mr. Piletta-Zanin need then?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than 10 minutes perhaps. We shall do our best to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break now. We'll adjourn until 11.00, and then I expect the cross-examination to be concluded in approximately 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please continue. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please Mr. President, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- my learned friend. May I, before my learned friend for the Defence recommences the cross-examination, just take the opportunity to announce the presence of Ms. Mahindaratne - I am sure I have the pronunciation correctly - Prashanthi Mahindaratne, who is now joining the Prosecution team in this matter. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome, Ms. Mahindaratne. I might have some difficulties in pronunciation, pronouncing your name, but I'll try to do my utmost best. Ms. Pilipovic, then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you told us yesterday that on the 11th of February, 1994, in early morning, you arrived in Sarajevo as a member of the team. Could you tell us who formed the commission for investigating the incident of the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: If I may correct, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Witness. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're feeling at home --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- pushing the buttons. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may correct what I said yesterday. On consulting my notes, I found that we did in fact arrive on the 10th but commenced work, as the learned defender has mentioned, early on the 11th. It was around 9.00 on the 11th when we commenced work. The commission at that time comprised the chief military observer, Brigadier General Gerardus Bastiaans, from Netherlands, who was replaced during the course of the day by Colonel Michel Gauthier, who subsequently signed the report. So the initial -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, I asked you who formed the commission, the name of the person who set up the commission of which you were a member.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was my understanding that it was set up by direction of the special representative for the Secretary-General, acting through the force commander to the Chief Military Observer, Brigadier General Gerardus Bastiaans.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you told us yesterday that you didn't examine the shrapnel because there was no evidence that the shrapnel came from the mine that actually exploded at the marketplace -- from the shell that exploded at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: By analysing the shrapnel by physical or chemical means, could it be established whether they come from one and the same shell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you examined the crater of the shell which fell on the marketplace in Sarajevo on the 5th of February. Could you tell us how deep the crater was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The crater was not very deep. If memory serves me, it was perhaps about ten centimetres deep. The fuse tunnel was somewhat more, perhaps 20, 30 centimetres, perhaps a little less.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, were you told whether a part of the fuse had been found?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the fuse found or a part of the fuse?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the velocity of the shell was or what it should have been and what it was to create the kind of crater that you saw at Markale?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The velocity of the shell isn't terribly relevant. When a mortar bomb is fired, as I mentioned yesterday, it gets a number of incremental charges, each of which gives a boost to its initial velocity. So depending on the charge that it's fired at will determine the velocity it comes down at. If it's fired with a large charge, it will rise very high in the air. It will come to a high vertex height and drop from there, and it is literally dropping. So the limiting factor would be air resistance. I mean, the rate of acceleration is standard. What is it? 9.81 metres per second, per second, but there is a terminal velocity. So it's not terribly relevant, to be quite honest. It can't be determined. There is no method of determination from which height the mortar fell and, therefore, no method of determining exactly what the initial velocity was and, therefore, what the charge was. It cannot be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, as you were talking about the charge, are you confirming your finding that it is impossible to establish from where the mine was fired because it is not known how many additional charges were used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is substantially correct. Because of the fact that it is impossible to determine, absolutely impossible to determine, the number of additional increments to the primary charge, then it is not possible with any sort of validity to say where the round was fired. However, what one can do if one has a good fuse tunnel and measures the incident angle, by consulting the range tables, one can work out six areas, in the case of a bomb like this which had six possibilities of different charges. If a mortar bomb had seven possibilities, for example, if it had seven charges, then there would be seven possible areas from which it could have been launched, all of them along the same line and all of them comprising effectively an oval area along that line, discrete from each other like pearls on a necklace, but well separated, if you can follow the analogy.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you were mentioning six possible positions. Is it possible, approximately, to establish the probability of hitting the Markale marketplace viewed from six possible firing positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is my view that in this particular case, due to the lack of adjusting rounds, that it was a fluke that the marketplace was hit. It was not necessarily the target. It may have been, but it may not have been. A mortar, particularly a 120-millimetre mortar which is not rifled, is not a terribly accurate weapon. It is an area weapon for suppression of activity over a wide area. It has a danger radius of about 500 metres. In other words, the splinters can travel up to 500 metres. It has technically got a lethal radius of 54 metres. That is, anyone who is not protected within 54 metres of the point of detonation is almost certain to suffer fatal wounds. But a mortar bomb, again, by its nature, because of the fact that it travels to a very high vertex height, it travels through different levels of atmosphere, where there are different temperature conditions, wind conditions, wind direction, for example, wind strength, all of which have an effect on what is a slow round. You can see a mortar bomb flying through the air. It is that slow. That is not possible with artillery weapons, but with a mortar bomb, it can be seen. Its time of flight is 30 to 45 seconds. And during that period, several different factors come into play, such as the wind speed, the wind direction, the air temperature, the temperature of the charge which fired it, barometric pressure. All these factors combine to make it an inaccurate round. Now, the fact that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you've just told us that it is possible to see the bomb flying. Could you tell us at what height it is possible to notice it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Generally, you'll see the bomb flying if you're behind the weapon, and you'll watch it for a period of maybe 15 seconds, up to about 15 seconds. But you have to be at the right angle. It can't be done normally from the side except in exceptional circumstances; from behind, because there is little apparent movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether the mine is fiery, like a fireball?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, not unless it's rocket-assisted. There's a specific type of round which is used which has a rocket to assist the achievement of a higher vertex height, and thus more range. But normal bombs, once they are fired, they are fired. The explosion occurs within the barrel, there's a large flash of fire at the mouth of the barrel, and that's it. The bomb is launched. It is inert as regards fire coming out of it or anything like that. It's merely a projectile at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, thank you. You mentioned six possible firing positions. My question is whether from all these potential positions of firing of the mentioned bomb, is the probability equal regarding hitting the Markale marketplace from each of these positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. Effectively, yes. The probability would be slightly higher the nearer the target is to the weapon. But not much. You're looking at approximately equal times of flight because of the fact that if the round is close, then generally it will be coming from a higher angle. So again, it takes a considerable period to fly through the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us with what degree of precision a bomb fired from a mortar can hit the set target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Providing that adjustment has occurred, that is, that previous bombs have been fired within the same general area, there are laid-down parameters. It must be within a time span of two hours. It must be left or right no more than, if I remember, about 150 mils, that is, say, 10 degrees. And it must be within certain range parameters. Then there is a good likelihood of hitting close to a target with a mortar bomb. But it is not an inherently accurate weapon in the same way that a gun or even a Howitzer is. It is difficult to get a round on target, extremely, extremely difficult to get a round on target, directly on target, even when the rounds have already been adjusted. There is still a certain amount of scatter. There is a beaten zone within which the round will land so many metres left and right, so many metres forward or backwards. In the case of a round being fired where there is no previous adjustment, it is extremely difficult to get -- it is almost certainly impossible to get a first-round hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, just one more question for you: On the basis of the sound produced by the bomb, is it possible to determine the direction and the position from which the bomb was fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Depending on the observer, he may hear the round being fired; and again, depending on the terrain, it may be possible to determine the general direction. But it will not be possible to determine a location, just direction. And again, you must take into account the fact that there may be terrain features in between, there may be buildings in between, there may be woods, for example, all of which would tend to muffle, mask, or deflect the sound. So really, it's an extremely inherently unreliable method. General direction is all that you will get.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, you examined the crater created at the Markale marketplace. Can a valid examination be done if the tunnel of the crater has been mechanically changed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was my view and my opinion on examining the fuse tunnel that it was inherently -- it was pretty well intact. It wasn't completely intact, but it was intact enough that I could make an estimate of the angle of incidence as being between 950 and 1.100 mils. That is within less than 10 degrees. A colleague of my mine put it to between 1.000 and 1.100 mils. I would say that the fuse tunnel was fairly intact. It was certainly intact enough to give us an angle of incidence which really proves nothing because, as I said, there are six possible locations from which that round could have been fired if those measurements were accurate, which I believe they were. But the measurement of the direction does not rely on the fuse tunnel method. There are other methods which we also used. We used different methods. And again, I would point out, madam, that there was remarkable consistency across the results despite the fact that each of us did our tests independently of the other and using different methods.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hamill, I have completed my part of the cross-examination. My colleague Piletta-Zanin has a few Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also remind Mr. Piletta-Zanin that where I indicated that -- where you indicated, yourself, that the cross-examining by Ms. Pilipovic would take another 10 minutes, it took approximately 20 minutes by now. So may I ask you to be as efficient as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning. I will express myself in French. Good morning. Do you know, sir, the name of Mr. Michael Rose? Is the name familiar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please bring the microphone closer to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether -- could you, sir, tell us whether Mr. Michael Rose was for a time responsible for UNPROFOR in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: General Michael Rose was the commander of BH command. That is, he was responsible for all UNPROFOR personnel in Bosnia i Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Do you know Mr. Divjak? Does the name sound familiar, Divjak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the name of one of your colleagues, that is Commander Jan Segers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I should like to show you two documents now, but before that, could you tell us if you know whether General Michael Rose wrote a book relating to his activities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: He did. I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was the title of that book "Fighting for Peace"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It may have been. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have here a copy of page 48 of this book which I should like to show to this witness and to read an extract from it. And may I do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Stamp. Are you aware of the existence of this book and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have copies to distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the book as the whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am aware of the existence book, and yesterday, my learned friend Ms. Pilipovic gave me a page from the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I imagine that is the same thing my friend Mr. Piletta-Zanin is referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the usher could assist me to distribute copies to everyone. I think there will be a sufficient number of copies. One for the witness and each of the parties. [In English] Oh, you can't have it. Mr. Usher, would you also take this one, please. Thanks. [Interpretation] I think the interpreters already have copies in the booth. Yes. Yes, I see them nodding. Yes. Thank you. Mr. President, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you page 4 [as interpreted]. I'm going to read the last paragraph on this page and to ask you a question about it. I will begin by reading, for the benefit of the booths --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I got page 48. I see reference here to page 4. Perhaps that's in error.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In French, I was talking about page 48.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We accept that it's a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So page 48, and I am reading the last paragraph. [In English] "Although the Serbs had now agreed virtually everything the Bosnians had asked for, Divjak was reluctant to sign up to a ceasefire, once again on the grounds that the UN proposal was not linked to any long-term political settlement. I told him that the people of Sarajevo would at that moment certainly settle for something short of this, just to be able to live in peace. He still would not agree. At this point I sprang a nasty surprise on him. I told him that the first UN examination of the bomb crater in Markale marketplace indicated that the bomb had been fired from the Bosnian side of the battle lines. The room went deadly silent and Hajrulakovic looked anxious. He coldly asked me to explain. I told him that the angle of the trajectory of the mortar bomb suggested that it had been fired at extremely short range from their side of the lines or perhaps detonated in situ. It was difficult, I said, to be precise when only one bomb had been fired and also because the Bosnian army had removed some of the important forensic evidence before the UN arrived." [Interpretation] End of quotation. Witness, could you please confirm that indeed, as far as you know, an important part of the evidence had been removed before the arrival of UN experts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Before I do that, may I say yes, the name of Divjak is now known to me now that I see it in context. Secondly, I would say that what General Rose said was nonsense in this extract. He obviously knew nothing about the operation of mortars, or else he was much more likely trying to make a political point and to further his negotiating position, but this -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you? I think the question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether General Rose was right when he said that part of the evidence was taken away before the UN arrived. As far as I understand your answer, you're commenting on his assessment of -- at least on the report of what was the source of fire of the mortar. I'd just like to avoid whatever confusion, because the statement contained several elements of information, and I think you're commenting on another one than the question was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
