utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Okay. From our investigation, from speaking to individuals who were on the scene, they were satisfied that no item was removed from the scene by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, are you sure? Are you sure that what is usually called the stabiliser had not been taken out before you arrived there and then put back in the place? When I say "before you arrived there," I mean the team.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It certainly happened before the team, because the team didn't arrive until the 11th of February. However, a team from FreBat was there shortly after the explosion, and a witness, a UN witness, had been present from within a very few minutes of the explosion. It is not conceivable in the confusion which occurred that any item would have been moved that quickly, before he saw what was happening. Our team interviewed several witnesses who had been there from practically the beginning and who were quite certain that there had been no disturbance. Again, I would suggest that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much. Let us try to be as brief as possible. Will you then tell me if -- if the stabiliser taken out or removed within the interval of several hours, if that had been the case, would it have affected your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Our conclusions were not quite as accurate as they might have been had the fin and tail section still been in situ when we arrived there. However, insufficient mechanical damage had been done to the crater to change what was actually written. What we wrote was written on the basis of what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, with regard to the shrapnel, when you said members of commission, did they ask to take possession of this evidence? And by "this" I mean shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: At the time, it was considered by the team leader that the shrapnel did not have integrity in that there was no definite chain linking the items, the shrapnel which were taken from the hole, from the crater, with the shrapnel that was shown to us. And in any event, the shrapnel was very, very small pieces which were insufficiently large to conduct an analysis by mechanical means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please try to show me with your fingers or with your hand what do you mean when you say too -- very small. Could you tell us what it is you understand as very small?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Indicated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, there were no larger pieces than that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not shown to us. Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Mr. President, let me say that the witness has made a gesture to show the space between his index finger and his thumb of about five [as interpreted] centimetres. I believe that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will now show you a photograph which you will get in a moment. This photograph has number ERN --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it might well be just a matter of the translation or what I heard. I think the translation has it here that Mr. -- my friend is putting -- it has "five centimetres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it now. I listened to the French version. What Mr. Piletta-Zanin said, in my recollection, is that it was one up to not more than two centimetres. Approximately one but not more than two. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, indeed that is what I did say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to show you an exhibit which has already been introduced, D61.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the usher please help me to show you. And we do not have a sufficient number of copies, so let me show it this way for everybody so everybody can see this document which we have already produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no copies, Mr. Usher, perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO so that everyone is better able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Usher, for your assistance. Could we please focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you a photograph which allegedly represents some of the fragments which were collected from the site. Could you confirm for us first that the scale which we have at the bottom here, that is a line in white and black, that the scale is in centimetres? That is, that every box, every square, means one centimetre. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It certainly appears that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And in relation to the shrapnel and the fragments which we are showing you, did you see fragments of this size of which some seem to be five to six centimetres long, if we can trust the scale below?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing such fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions regarding that photograph, Mr. President. It can be removed from the ELMO. I'm simply trying to be as fast as possible. Now I'd like to show another document which has number D79, 7-9. I believe that we have also given the text to the interpreters so as to allow everybody to understand me better. But we can give it to everybody, and I will keep one copy of it. I do not know if the booths have the document. No, the interpreters do not. So we shall need three copies for the booth, Usher, please. [In English] Would you bring some for the translation booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me wait for 30 seconds so that the booths can get this copy. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Witness, you have before you a document which has the stamp of the United Nations, and it seems that it has some French abbreviations and also English abbreviations. Do you recognise this type of document? Could you just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you have never seen this type of document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, the name that you can see at the bottom of this document and the names -- these names are Anne Mawis - and I'm not sure that I'm pronouncing them properly - and Marc Le Nouaille, are they familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I know neither name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And the name of General Briquemont, which you can see on page 5, does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I know General Briquemont. He was the commander of BH command - in other words, all UN forces - in Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Francois Briquemont, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed, thank you. Witness, since you are an expert in these matters, could you tell us what does "SMIO" mean that we see at the top on the left-hand side, the second line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: SMIO stands for "senior military information officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So we are talking about a relatively high-ranking officer, are we?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So we are talking about a low-ranking officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: All UNMOs should be of the rank of captain or major. The job of SMIO in UNMO HQ in Zagreb varied. Sometimes it was a major, sometimes it was a captain. And on one occasion that I'm aware of, it was a major who just got promoted to lieutenant colonel. So UNMOs do tasks. This is one of the tasks that is done by UNMOs. The SMIO worked for me in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have one or perhaps two paragraphs, and I'd like to read them, if I have your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We find it on page 4, and that is indeed page 4, third paragraph, rather, the third chapter, and it begins, "Even the Muslim Bosnians..." That is the question. And I will be quoting from letters JS. These are the initials of Mr. Jan Segers who was at the SMIO that we are talking about. I am beginning the quote: [In English] "... the shelling of their own people. In particular, the terrible massacres at the marketplace in Sarajevo. Concerning the first one, in February 1994, which killed 70 persons, UN always have told that they didn't know who were the responsibles. Nevertheless, it was quite sure that it were not the Serbs. Some rumours mentioned that it were explosives who were put under a table... Concerning the last shell on the marketplace, the one just before the NATO massive air strikes against the Serbs, the spokesman of the UN confirmed that the projectile was coming from their lines. But the UNMO who did the investigation immediately after the catastrophe, as well as other UN officers who did an investigation, have stated that it was possible that the projectile was fired from the Moslem side. Of course, the ballistic and crater analysis are not an exact science. And we all know very well that we are manipulated: Local authorities are using us in their own interest. When we are telling something that you don't have to say, we are threatened or expulsed." [Interpretation] End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you two questions: This is a text which was produced by Mr. Jan Segers, and it mentioned the existence of rumours. Did you personally hear any such rumours?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you then tell us under what circumstances did you hear those rumours?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I mentioned in my testimony yesterday, for example, the story that was given to us by a captain of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps headquarters that the projectile had been launched pneumatically from an address maybe 150 metres from the marketplace. That was one. The second one was we were told there was a bomb placed in the marketplace and this was detonated, and the mortar bomb didn't, in fact, exist. Another one was that the mortar bomb was used as a cover for the detonation of an explosive device in the marketplace. All of these were total and utter nonsense. This piece of paper is also similarly nonsense. Rumours are rumours. Fact is fact. The analysis was a complete and thorough analysis and was accurate and stated exactly what we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My last question -- thank you for this answer. And my very last question: So this United Nations officer says that he was aware to a certain extent that they, or we - I mean the UN staff - were, and I quote it again, "manipulated." Was that your impression, too, at times?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It depends on your definition of "manipulation." What I would say about that is that it was quite clear that the competing factions of every side, not just in Bosnia but also in Croatia, in Macedonia, wherever, would use the United Nations to its own best effect, naturally. But we were aware that such a thing was happening. And indeed, there had to be a certain flexibility in our operation; otherwise, we couldn't have achieved what we did achieve. So certainly there were attempts to manipulate us. Of course there were. I was present. I was an attempted victim of manipulation. But once one is aware that people are trying to manipulate one, then one can deal with it. It's not a problem. It's a fact of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to those witnesses that you mentioned and these problems of manipulation, a moment ago, I heard you say that Sarajevo troops, the so-called government troops, had deployed mortars in the immediate proximity of the Kosevo Hospital. Could you, yourself, see them since you were outside that particular -- outside the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I could not. But this information was given to us by our colleagues on the Papa side, that is, the UNMOs who worked on the side inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you consider this information reliable?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions, Mr. President. Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need for the Prosecution to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, just one or two matters of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that sniping, in normal military parlance, means a concealed person, operating independently, shooting from a distance with optical devices for assistance. You also spoke of sniping in a more general sense from, for example, the Bristol Hotel into Grbavica. Having regard to what -- to those two comments you made, I'd like you to have a look at Document P3675. And let me ask you for one clarification.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know to what you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 8 of that document, at K. Could you just read that paragraph quickly and I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly. "Sniping, a term used indiscriminately in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia applied usually to the targeting of civilians with a variety of single-shot and multiple-shot [machine-guns] weapons. The expression derives from the fact that the source of fire is usually so well concealed that it is difficult to pinpoint. Sniping in the military sense is conducted for specific purposes, sometimes using specialised weapons that are expressly designed for sniping. Sniping in the Balkan context is against a civilian population that is neither capable of protective measures nor equipped for an appropriate repast. Snipers in NATO armies undergo an extensive selection and training regime." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you agree with me that that passage explains two different context in which you have used the expression "sniping"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. As I said yesterday, sniping normally applies to firing single shots against specific targets. There is, in artillery terms, a term called a "sniping gun" which is a single-gun action against a pinpoint target, and that would be closer to the definition of sniping as used here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that would be sniping in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Well, they are both sniping in the military sense. They both are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: But the normal sniping that we refer to refers to an individual with a specific one-shot weapon with optical enhancement, firing from a concealed position at a target, at a specific target.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you -- you spoke about or you were asked about the incident at the waterline on the -- in July 1993. Can you recall where you were on the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I can. I was actually in Radava at the time, negotiating with the headquarters staff of the Kosevo Brigade, so I was on the very far side of the city on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked questions about the incident of the 1st of June, 1993, and you said that you learned about it at the time, you can't remember exactly from whom, but you would certainly have learned about it, if nowhere else, from CNN, which gave you a lot of information. Where would you have received this type of information about that shelling from CNN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm making an assumption that I may have seen it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that. But where, if you had received it from CNN, would you be viewing CNN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Inside the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At which barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In PTT. Now, we also had television in Lukavica, but generally we watched television Republika Srpska, or from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. You said that the UNMO --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry. I also had the World Service on my radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. BBC World Service.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's in evidence. Thanks very much. You said that the UNMO personnel were inadequate right through the former Yugoslavia, including in and out of Sarajevo. Having regard to that, would the UNMOs be in a position to record all the artillery fire from any side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. As I indicated, we were in very short supply. At one period, we were down to five observers for the entire southern sector of the city. This was totally insufficient. We had to close some of our locations at times because of the dearth of observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from that, I take it there would have been a substantial amount of fire which would have escaped UNMO observation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Fire would have escaped observation, but in general terms, there would have been a team located sufficiently close to hear firing going on and to report it. That is not to say that we recorded every single engagement or every single round fired in every single engagement. That would have been beyond our capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said - and perhaps I heard you incorrectly - that Mount Igman, among other places, was under the control of the Bosnian army throughout the conflict, yet I recall you saying that at one stage in the conflict it had been captured by one party. Could you just explain that? Was it under the control of --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- any party throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was under the control -- Igman itself was under the control initially of the Bosnian government, that is President Izetbegovic's government. However, as I indicated, around the 19th of July, a battle commenced on Igman, during which the troops of the Igman Brigade and the Ilidza Brigade attacked Igman and captured it. It was taken by them. The UN stepped in, forced a ceasefire and patrolled the area on the top. At one stage, however, the UN withdrew from certain positions and they were reoccupied by the army of the BH government, that is, President Izetbegovic's government. So that they had it for most of the conflict. They had it taken from them for a period - not all of Igman now, they still had part of the mountain, it's a big mountain - and then they retook peacefully, they reoccupied an area which had been evacuated by UN troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the Kosevo hospital incident --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- did you do a formal and complete investigation of that incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did not. I formed an impression of what I saw on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did not -- I did not do a complete analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you are not sure but you believe the fuse or a part of the fuse was found. If that was found and that came to the attention of the UNPROFOR team, would that have been recorded in the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: As I think about it, I think it's quite possible that we didn't find it, because if we had done, I'm sure I would have remarked on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I think I may have been mistaken in saying that it was found by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it that you did not remark on it in the report which you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- penned.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the fragments that you saw were a certain size, which you indicated. From your report, there were two sets of fragments. There was one which were found inside the fuse tunnel. That one set, you had already indicated it was very small. And there were some fragments which were shown to members of the team by the Bosnian representatives, by the representatives of the Federation. Can you recall if you were present among the members of the UNPROFOR team at the meeting where that set of fragments was shown?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do recall. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The fragments, therefore, which you saw which were too small would have been the other set of fragments which were taken from the crater?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. May I say that the head of the team who saw the fragments told us that the fragments which were in the possession of the authorities told us that they were not usable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that mortars are normally set up, fired, a few rounds will be fired, and then they are moved. Could you briefly explain to us, in the normal operation of a mortar where it is used in the shoot-and-scoot fashion, to use your terms, what would be adjusting rounds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: A mortar goes into position. The best available data meteorologically and ballistically would be fed into a computer which would then calculate an elevation and a bearing to fire the mortar on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you always have to use a computer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, you don't. No, no, not at all. You can do it by eye. If you can see the target, you can do it by eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is there --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Or you can use other means. There are other aids.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm simply asking you how the concept of adjustment works where the mortar is shooting and scooting.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: What happens is there has to be an observer who can see the fall of shot, that is, where the rounds land. When the first round is fired from the mortar, the observer reports back to somebody on the gun line, normally a command-post officer who mans the command post which calculates the data, where the round has come down in relation to the target and in relation to himself. At that stage, the person in the command post takes that information, translates it into technical data, into a new bearing and a new elevation and possibly a new charge, and fires the weapon again. The second round then comes somewhat closer but probably not on target. Again the observer reports back the new impact area, gives a correction, and that is applied on the gun. At that stage, the mortar commander will fire several rounds from all his tubes and then pack up and go away. Normally, he would fire five rounds per tube.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at that stage, having fired these earlier rounds, he would be on target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the earlier rounds are called adjusting rounds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And having come on target, they would pack up and leave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Having done what the observer wanted them to do to the target, they would pack up and go, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You were based in Zagreb, I take it, when you were asked to go to the market for investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it that the -- your evidence is that the mortars of the Bosnian Serb army and the artillery in general was always normally placed at one set position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. They very, very rarely moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, may we take advantage of the presence of Mr. Hamill for him to give us a definition of a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think he gave a definition, more or less, and then confronted with a definition which was not exactly the same. But in your view, Mr. Hamill, did you give us a definition of a sniper? Because we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my belief, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that I did several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's my recollection as well. But if there's any specific element perhaps on that definition that you'd like to put an additional question, I'll be -- but if you just ask for a definition, I expect Mr. Hamill to tell you the same as he did before.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the range of a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It depends on the weapon he's firing. I mean, a sniper rifle can fire to 1.000 metres very, very accurately. If the optical instrument on the rifle is calibrated and is strong enough, he can take out a person's head at 1.000 metres with a rifle. With a gun, on the other hand, it is dependent on what the layer of the gun, the person who is actually sighting the gun, can see. He must be able to see his target. And again, that is the essence of sniping, that you see the target that you are firing at. You must locate that target, you must use a telescopic instrument to lay your cross-hairs on that target, and then you fire on it. So it's -- the definition of sniping, effectively, is firing on a seen, specified target. That's -- that's in its basic element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, I will ask my colleagues whether they have any questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. I won't take too much time, you must be tired, but I would like to go back to what we referred to as snipers. According to your knowledge and experience, do you have the impression that these snipers acted within the framework of a strategy or was it, rather, individual actions that were not coordinated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is my belief that snipers operated as a tool of the management, as it were, and they were there for a specific purpose, and they were under the control of somebody -- somebody in authority, so that there was a strategy for using snipers as an instrument of terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us go on now to the shots that targeted the Markale marketplace. If I understood correctly, there was a single shot, a single shell that hit the market. In your opinion, was it possible to target the market with a single round without prior adjustment, regardless of who may have done the firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was -- it would have been an extremely lucky shot for the firer if he had hit the target that he was aiming at first time around, for a number of reasons. There had been no firing in the area for some considerable time, certainly well outside two-hour time limit that we allow for. In my view, that particular round was not necessarily aimed at the market but was aimed somewhere in the general area of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your testimony, you use the expression or definition, that is, the notion of Chetniks. What do you mean by the word "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: A Chetnik, Your Honour, was a royalist soldier during the Second World War. However, during the Yugoslav secession wars, the expression became used for a Serb irregular, that is, a soldier of a militia not directly or apparently not directly under the control of the governing authorities of one of the entities which was conducting military operations. That's why I used the term "so-called Chetnik" rather than "Chetnik." In this particular case in Sarajevo, there was a band of irregulars which I believed to be under the control of a particular officer. This band was led by one Vasilije Vidovic, and their object was to spread terror throughout the area and to prevent entry into specified areas, generally to the north and east of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You spoke of them as being allies of the army, allies of the VRS. Is there any institutional relationship? Were they subject to directives or orders from the regular army, or were they totally independent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is my view that they were tools of the regular army used for specific purposes, used for purposes which would be illegal normally. And they were -- they could be disowned, as it were. The authorities could disown them, could disclaim responsibility for their activities and claim that they were outside control. I was asked yesterday about uniforms and I said that the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, wore a kind of brown-green camouflage uniforms. The irregulars, the so-called Chetniks, did not wear such uniform. They wore black clothes or perhaps civilian clothes. They were not dressed in appropriate uniform. But again, as I say, my view was they were used as a tool of the authorities to conduct operations which could be disowned, "black" operations, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but my last question is that you said that in your opinion, the shells that hit the hospital came from a tank. Is that true? Did both sides have the opportunity to drive tanks around in that part of the town?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. Only one side, the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had access to that area. From recollection, I would say that the VRS had not got access to -- they had no possibility of firing tanks at that hospital at that time. There was a range of hills in between their positions and the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the tank was close to the hospital, was it not, and was moving around under protection or, in your opinion, can a tank move without being protected? Because other witnesses have said that, in military terms, tanks normally need protection. They don't circulate. They don't move around individually alone.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Normally, Your Honour, tanks would move in troops of three or four as part of a squadron of 12 or 14, as part of a regiment and so on. However, as I mentioned, the Armija BH were extremely short of heavy hardware such as tanks and artillery and they used them in an unconventional method as did, indeed, the VRS use their equipment in an unconventional method. This is not a classic war as we have seen on the various battlefields of Europe or the Middle East. This is more akin to a siege wherein you had an area inside and an area outside a front line, the front line remaining effectively in the same place for most of the period. So that a tank, if moving inside, was moving within its own protected area in that sense, or if it were outside, if it were, for example, on the hill of Gornja Mladica, it was moving in an area which was under the control of the appropriate authorities to which it responded, so that it was certainly easy, in that sense, for a tank to move around inside the area in Zetra stadium, for example, or that general area without interference from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also a few questions, Mr. Hamill. First, just for my better understanding, you testified yesterday about sniping, I would say, in the area of Grbavica and Hrasno. You told us that there was sniping coming into Grbavica from the armija side, as you told us. Was that sniping fire always received at the other side of the front line, or did you ever experience that sniping fire was coming from and received at the same side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The sniping generally took place on the front line itself. There were blocks of flats in the lower Grbavica area leading on to the River Miljacka and other buildings, shops and so on. And they tended to be the target of the snipers, or those people in those areas tended to be the targets of the snipers. So that it was clearly coming from the other side of the river. It was coming from the area controlled by the armija. Sometimes incendiary rounds were used; sometimes small arms were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the whole Grbavica area was controlled --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: By the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you never noticed any, I would say, sniping that stayed within one side of the front line? Well, let's say BiH sniping fired --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: VRS to VRS, no. No, oh, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you never noticed any intentional civilian objects being targeted when you were, I think, at your Lima posts. Were you usually aware of what the targets would be? You explained to us also that you would be informed about the targets.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you always informed? In how many per cent of the cases were you informed about any firing? You would be informed about the target and also perhaps in how many per cent of the cases you were not informed at all about fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Firing was always reported because of the fact that a team was living on the firing site or close to it. So there was no way of firing without the team not being aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: So they told us what they were firing at. They told us perhaps it was in response to an attack on certain positions or certain villages or areas. Invariably, the firers would tell the team which would be supervising them, as it were, which would be monitoring them, what they were firing at. But would always claim, of course, that it was a military target, and there would be no way of verifying what was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could not, by reading the reports later on, the increps, see whether the target mentioned to you were also actually the targets where the shells or the projectiles landed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. President, there was a lot of firing going on at the time, and we were more interested in providing reports than in reading them. I cannot recall any instance of sitting down and correlating one to the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then have to understand your testimony, if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you say that you never noticed any targeting of civilian objects, that you were never told civilian objects to be targeted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On a question of Judge El Mahdi, you told us that, in your view, sniping was used as an instrument by the -- let me perhaps just read your words.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: By the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, by the authorities. And I do understand, the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Military and civilian, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Military and civilian, yes. Could you tell us on what this view is based? You told us it was your view, but what's the basis of your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is based on the fact that it continued throughout the period from April 1992 until the end of hostilities. And if the political and military authorities had wished, they could have stopped sniping. They didn't obviously so wish. Therefore, they were, at the very least, encouraging it. And in my view, the direct follow-on, the logical follow-on, is that they were using it as an instrument of terror against the opposing side. I would say that there was sufficient control over the area, there was sufficient control over the military by the political end, and there was sufficient control over the lower military units by the higher military formations, that they could have stopped any illegal activity of that nature had they so wished. They did not do so. The firing continued. The sniping continued. Civilians kept getting targeted. Therefore, it must have been a decision made or else a non-decision made not to stop them. Either way, it was policy that they would use snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another question in a total different area. You explained to us the -- I would say the adjustment mechanism in firing mortars. You would first fire one round, then see where it lands, and then... Could you tell us: An experienced, a well-trained crew, in their first effort, so in their first adjusting round, how close would they, at an average, come to a target? I mean, would it be 200 metres, 500 metres, 1 kilometre? Because you said the second round could come closer. So I'd like to know what would be approximately the diversion range of the first round, and then perhaps of the second round.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Given good map data and given good meteorological data and map spotting and computation, it should be within 2 or 300 metres of the target. The second one would be a lot closer, perhaps on the other side of the target, less than half that distance. And then the third one would generally be on or about the target. And again, as I mentioned, a mortar bomb has a very wide area of damage, so that if it's within a hundred metres, it can be considered to be -- with 120, it can be considered to be a target round because you will cause the disruption that you require at 100 metres. So say 300, say 100, and next you're right on target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You told us about the damage you saw I think it was in the Kosevo Hospital which you expected to have been fired from a tank, rather horizontally.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The impact came from what side; the north, south, east, west?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: It would have been from the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the north.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: From the north. Generally from the north. Again, I wasn't examining my compass, but it was a general northerly direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you're talking about the hills, these are the hills north of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: The hills north of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us that an untrained ear could not distinguish between any kind of explosion. Did you have specific explosions in mind? I mean, a normal rifle is also kind of an explosion in it. That's my first question, what type of explosions you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my second question would be what would training on the spot for one, two, or three years by civilians do to their ability to make a distinction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: For the first part, my understanding of the context was that it was the difference between a shell fired from a gun or Howitzer and a bomb fired from a mortar, and it was in that context that I said an untrained ear would not be able to tell the difference between them, or perhaps even an explosion caused by explosives being detonated or a mine being detonated. Now, the population of Sarajevo was subject to rigorous training during a very long period of time, and I'm quite sure that they would have fine-tuned their senses. However, there is no difference really between the sound made by a shell and a bomb. It's just a very large rolling bang. But it's quite different to the sound made by a gun or a mortar firing. They would certainly hear a difference there after a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from the firing of the explosive itself, would the way it moves through the air make a different sound? We heard testimony before about whistling sounds or -- could you explain to us what would be the difference and what an untrained or a trained-on-the-spot ear could deduct from what we hear?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: You are quite right, Mr. President, when you mention the whistling sound. This is caused by the fact that when a shell is fired from a gun, it goes through the barrel and is twisted as it is moving, because there is rifling, that is, there are grooves twisted through the barrel to give it spin. And the spin is required to stabilise the round to make it fly in a straight line. Without spin, it would wobble and thus not be accurate. So what you're hearing is the sound of the shell rotating as it's going through the air. And also the fact is that guns in particular are fired at very high muzzle velocities. They are very fast. So you get a crack as well, which would be equivalent to a sonic bomb. You get this crack, you get the whistle. A mortar bomb on the other hand, because of the nature of the weapon, is fired from a much lighter type barrel and using lower pressure explosives so that it goes off with a whomp. And as it flies through the air, there's no spin. The reason there's no spin is because there's no rifling on the barrel to give it spin. In place of rifling to give it stability, it has a tail with fins on it, six, eight, or ten fins, whatever number of fins the makers deem it requires. So this -- these fins stabilise it in flight, and it is practically silent. Because of its slowness and lack of spin, practically silent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you finally give us -- you told us about the shootreps and the increps, and you mentioned a couple of times the differences between the factions. Could you give us an indication as far as either shelling or perhaps even sniping is concerned what was the balance between one of the parties firing? Would it be 50/50? 40/60, 70/30 and in --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: In general terms, there were far more shootreps, far more - maybe ten times as many shootreps - from the -- no, sorry, maybe not ten. But certainly considerably more times shooting from the VRS side than from the armija side. The shooting from the VRS side tended to be of a heavier nature, that is, artillery weapons or mortars. There was a much heavier concentration of small-arms fire came from the armija side, the Armija BH side. Now, small-arms fire would generally go unremarked in the daily reports. The only things which went into the daily reports were heavy, very heavy, small-arms fire which would indicate a battle, or shelling. And as the shelling came predominantly from - 90 per cent probably - from the VRS side, there seemed in the reports to be a major imbalance in that way. But again, the VRS used artillery in the same way that the armija used infantry. The VRS was infantry light. They didn't have the troops, so they needed the artillery as a force multiplier to make up for the lack of troops. On the other side, the armija had masses of troops but little by way of heavy weapons, so they used the small-arms much more heavily than the VRS would have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. And final question is you told us about mortar positions held just perhaps very short time at Kosevo Hospital and at the UN building. We have heard testimony before about one report of a mortar firing from the Kosevo Hospital. You used the plural. Could you give us more information about the other occasions where it happened, apart from one that was reported, at least according to the testimony given in this Court.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. President, that was anecdotal evidence which I got socially from our colleagues on the Papa side. So I couldn't give specific instances, dates, times. But there were -- in conversation, it would have been said that it happened on a number of occasions. Now, again, we're talking maybe two, maybe five. I don't know. It's purely anecdotal evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's similarly true for the UN headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I only remember one specific instance, because I came into the headquarters either that day or the day after and it was said to me, "They've done it again. They were firing from the car park." So the word "again" was used, indicating that it was not the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Yes. I was about announcing a break, Mr. Ierace, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- I'd seek Your Honour's -- your leave to ask one question by way of clarification of an answer given by the witness to a question asked from the Bench. It is simply a question of clarification and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please put the question. We'll then have a break, of course, after the -- if there's any question -- do you have any additional questions on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would also have a point of clarification. It may have been the -- it may be the same one as Mr. Ierace. Who knows?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... from other side, from both sides, or perhaps the same question. We could do it before the break. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that there were bands of irregulars who, in your opinion, came under the control of the authorities. You referred to one band who you said you believed to be under the control of a particular officer and that the band was led by one Vasilije Vidovic. Do you mean by that that the officer's name was Vasilije Vidovic or was that someone else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. In this particular case, the leader of the band was Vasilije Vidovic. However, it was my belief - I was told by my interpreter - that he was under the control of another officer, an officer who was, in fact, as far as I know, a brigade commander and commander of the -- a kind of interim or intermediate commander of various brigades on the northern side of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you told the name of that officer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I was. I was told that his name was General Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it the same question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, because after all, this was three questions, not just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a doubt to accept your estimations as far as the time is concerned. If you tell us that you can do it really in a couple of minutes, I'll give you the opportunity now, otherwise we'll first have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be as brief as the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you spoke a moment ago about the authorities' control over a group of snipers. When giving your personal assessment, because this was an assessment, did you also have in mind the -- the so-called Sarajevo troops and the Sarajevo authorities, that is, the government authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, for being so clear and precise. My second question: Witness, in relation to the question of snipers, had you heard of an anti-sniper agreement or at least a draft agreement which was elaborated in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have some memory of such discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it General Galic, who is here present, who was the initiator on the Serb side of this draft?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, we don't have the answer to the question about -- when it says: "When giving your personal assessment because this was an assessment, did you also have in mind the so-called Sarajevo troops and the Sarajevo authorities, that is, the government authorities?" talking about the sniping. You said, "Of course," or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENDAN HAMILL
utterances.text: Exactly. "Of course." I said, "Of course."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't check in the transcript but that's also what in my recollection was that you -- yes. The answer is not -- at the end of line 20 of page 72, there's an "A" for answer but the answer was, "Of course," you said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to confirm that, because perhaps we were speaking too quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This concludes your testimony in this court. I thank you very much for answering questions of all the parties and questions of the Bench. You will understand that it is important for this Court to have the information from those who are present at these times and these places in order to prepare the decisions it will have to take. So thank you once again very much for coming. Mr. Usher, could you please lead Mr. Hamill out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to the parties that since it's twenty minutes to one that we first have a break until 1.00 and then deal with the documents. We'll adjourn until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would first like to go through the documents. But if there's anything you'd like to raise before we come to the documents, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I do, Mr. President. To begin with, I should like to apologise to the Chamber for being unable to be present yesterday. But I'm quite sure that my colleague Ms. Pilipovic has explained the reasons. Now, Mr. President, the Defence wishes to say the following: We have already raised it before you on different occasions, and reiterate that a document which it considers indispensable for the Defence, and these are the documents which principally are of military nature, either what we call here directives coming from headquarters to -- from the main staff to army corps and so on and so forth. You have this witness who knows a great deal about Sarajevo, even though he was there for a very short time. However, the Defence has still not received the documents which exist, and therefore we were unable to ask all the questions of this witness simply because it was denied - and I'm using that word - denied access to documents to which the Prosecution knows exist, (a); and (b), where they exist. When I say where, it is one floor away from here. And we were completely handicapped in conducting our Defence. Perhaps it was shorter, so that is perhaps good, but on the other hand, the Defence would have been better, and that is not a good thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber expects to be informed on short notice about the new developments in this area, and we are -- we have taken notice of your objection that you have not received yet the documents, or at least, have access to those documents you would need for proper cross-examining also the witness of today. That's how I understand your position. We'll keep a close eye on it. And of course, we have taken decisions before on how to proceed, and we'll see what's the outcome of that. Madam Registrar, would you then please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2261, UNPROFOR investigation report. P226.2, "Examination of the Crater at Sarajevo Market" report. Exhibit P2261A, "Sarajevo Market Explosion of 5 February, 1994, a Background Summary of UNPROFOR's Investigative Report." P3675, "Weaponry in the former Yugoslavia" report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think one of the questions is that whether the translation of this report is tendered as well or it's just given for the information of the other party. I don't remember to have received the translation of the report. I don't know what the Prosecution intended. Well, Mr. Stamp is not there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure where Mr. Stamp is. There may have been a misunderstanding as to the timing of the tendering of the exhibits. I wonder whether we could leave the tendering of the exhibits until five minutes before we finish this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although I clearly indicated that it would be the first thing to do after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather proceed. I've heard no objections whatsoever, and the only thing still to be decided is whether 3675.1 is tendered as well, because that's the B/C/S version of the same report. We have not been provided with a translation, and I think the Chamber would have difficulties anyway in reading the B/C/S version. So if it was just a translation for the benefit of better understanding by General Galic, then...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have a copy of the report with a translation. Excuse me, Mr. President. That is a translation into B/C/S as well as the English original version. If that assists with the tender, the translation, of course, is P3675.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but do you want to tender the translation as well? It has not been provided to the Chamber. You have one, and I don't know whether it's just a matter of...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand it, there was some indication from the Bench yesterday that a copy wasn't required. But in any event, I am able to provide copies for each member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether you want to tender the translated version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you want to. That's then 3675.1. Could you please further guide us, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know whether the Defence had this translation. I wasn't here yesterday, but I do not believe -- I do not think that this translation was given to the evidence [as interpreted]. But whatever the case, I'd like -- I'd like to cast an eye for what I've received. Yes, I had the instruction from my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please ask the usher to give the extra copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to check the channel. I asked for the translation into English, but perhaps I wasn't quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a misunderstanding, because I was talking about the translation in B/C/S. And I can imagine that you and not Ms. Pilipovic are in a position to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the English text, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Prosecution will provide you with an English text, or it will be given to you by the usher now. If there's any objection to be made, you can do it at a later stage. We're just talking about -- on the other hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please guide us further, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D77, map marked by witness; Exhibit D78, excerpt from book "Fighting for Peace" by General Sir Michael Rose; Exhibit D79, UNPROFOR report, article written by Jan Segers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask for clarification, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The names under the Article, Ann Mawis and Marc Le Nouaille, on the top, it says: "Written by Commander Jan Segers," but the content of the document seems to be something like an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. What I understand as regards this document is -- is that it is the record which was done by Ms. -- by the two undersigned of a statement or an article which appeared in Tele Moustique, which is a weekly, if I understand well, and the date is the 30th of November, 1995, and in which Mr. Jan Segers participated, so that that is why he appears as the author. And these are the excerpts from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do object to the tender of D79 for these reasons: that when one looks at the document, it purports to be, and I stress that, a reprint of an excerpt from a Belgian weekly paper which appeared on the 30th of November, 1995. The witness has taken to the document as a whole and asked whether he recognised that type of document. He did not. He was asked whether he knew of Jan Segers. He did not. Indeed, the only point of agreement between the witness and the Defence was that he was aware of the existence of General Briquemont. There is no basis for the document to be tendered. The witness was invited to comment on a particular passage which appears in the document that was read to him. So it's on the record. So by the document not coming into evidence, the integrity of the evidence otherwise is not impaired. There is no basis for the document to be tendered, in my respectful submission, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it's true that you read the whole part you asked any comment on to the witness, which was on page 4, the third paragraph. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is quite true, Mr. President. On the other hand, Mr. Ierace omitted to say that the major question why we showed the witness this document, why we're producing it, that it comes from the United Nations, that is, UNPROFOR, and because it refer to the existence of rumours and manipulation. And the witness had answered that that was it. And therefore, I believe that it is relevant. And we intend to show it to another witness again to ask him if the -- if UNPROFOR produced these kind of documents or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I agree with you that it is saying "UNPROFOR" at the top. It seems to be a kind of an extract from or a whole article from a text. So if you would expect to -- for example, the ICTY to take responsibility for whatever is in the press clippings which is distributed sometimes, then of course that's a different thing. Press clippings are -- this looks very much like press clippings. And if you're talking about manipulation and about rumours, that's exactly the part that was read to the witness. So -- but let me just confer with my colleagues to see what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the decisions usually taken in respect of previous statements given by witnesses, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and since only a small part of the document which has been read by you to the witness has been dealt with during the cross-examination, the Chamber decides that the objection should be sustained and that all relevant parts of the document and the existence of the document are covered and are in the transcript. So the -- the document is not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let it be so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I call Witness AH. I indicate in advance that the witness will in due course be shown some photographs. It would be appropriate, in my respectful submission, for those photographs to be dealt with in a way in which they cannot be viewed publicly because of a signature on them and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- some individuals who appear on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will keep a close eye on that. Witness AH is protected by pseudonym, face, and voice distortion. May I expect that the voice distortion has been prepared properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am informed that the voice distortion is not yet properly prepared, so we'll have to have a break for five, up to ten minutes in order to test whether the voice distortion is effective or not. Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Before we take that break, I should merely like to note one thing that I've just discovered, and that is that the English translation seems that I know -- but that there are some modifications, some changes in hand, by hand. But I see -- no. No, observation. There are initials here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you should have conferred with lead counsel, because he could have explained to you that part of the testimony was specifically on this handwritten. So will you please, first, if you have not been present during the examination, first confer with lead counsel and only then make any observations. We will have a break for five, up to ten minutes, until the voice distortion has been properly prepared. --- Break taken at 1.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I call Witness AH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is proper care taken that while entering the courtroom, the face of the witness will not be shown to the outside world? I'm asking for confirmation to the technical booth. Could I please get a confirmation that when the witness is entering the courtroom, that her face will not be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is confirmed to me. Since -- is there anyone in the public gallery? No. So please, Mr. Usher, would you escort the witness to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could it be a little louder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question to you. Could you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're nodding. Would you please give an answer aloud, because when you nod it will not be understood by the interpreters and it will not be translated, and therefore it will not be in the transcript. So whenever I ask a question, or if anyone else asks you a question, would you please give an audible answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. AH, I'll not call you by your own name because protective measures are granted in respect of you. So therefore, I'll address you as "Ms. AH." Before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. AH, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. You'll then be examined by counsel for the Defence. So please, Mr. Ierace, would you proceed. And may I remind both parties to put off their microphones when the witness is answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P3676.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does the piece of paper in front of you correctly record your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Do you have a brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before that exhibit is taken from the table in front of the witness, with the leave of the Bench, I seek that the witness writes on the same piece of paper the name of her brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
